messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ravi is a 75-year-old potter, a South Asian man who fled his home country during a period of ethnic cleansing decades ago. The memory of the journey refuses to settle into language. What he carries is not a story but a series of fragments—the wet dirt of a mass grave he was forced to help dig, the sudden crack of gunfire that sounded like a car backfiring, the sight of soldiers’ boots approaching as he pressed his face into the earth. These pieces do not connect; they arrive without sequence, and when they come, they feel more real than the present moment. He cannot describe them in sentences. When his wife asks what is wrong, he shakes his head. The words will not come.

Now he lives in a small American city, working clay in a studio behind his house. For years the wheel was his refuge. But after a nephew’s funeral two months ago—his first visit to a cemetery since the trauma—Ravi felt something shift. Standing before the grave, the smell of turned earth and the sight of headstones collapsed into that old pit. His legs gave way. He had to be helped to the car. Since then, he has avoided any situation that might remind him of grief or endings. When an invitation to a community art show arrives, he throws it out; the thought of being praised, of feeling hopeful, frightens him in a way he cannot explain. He tells himself that hoping is dangerous, that it invites disaster. He has come to believe he is no longer capable of the steady, joyful work that once defined him. Even the slightest upset—a dish that cracks in the kiln—makes him put down his tools and walk away, certain he cannot cope with one more thing going wrong.

The connection between his constant vigilance and the intrusions is tight. Ravi scans his environment without meaning to. When he hears a car backfire, his body seizes before his mind can catch up; the sound becomes a gunshot, and for a long moment he is back in that field. The police cruiser that parks down the street sends him into the kitchen, pulse racing. He now avoids any potential confrontation with his wife or neighbors; if a disagreement begins, he leaves the room, because arguing feels like the first step toward violence. These avoidances, however, only deepen his conviction that he is fragile, that the world is saturated with risk. His scanning makes him more sensitive; he notices a car idling, a uniformed figure, a patch of freshly turned earth, and each such perception triggers another wave of appraisal—*I cannot handle this, I must be on guard*—which in turn summons a fragment of memory: the taste of mud, the sound of boots.

The memories, especially the fragmented ones, dictate his behavior. He refuses to listen to the radio because news reports might mention funerals or war. He will not drive with his wife past the cemetery. The check of his surroundings has become second nature; before he steps into the hardware store, he peers through the window for any man in dark clothing. This vigilance once helped him survive the escape, but now it makes every walk feel like a patrol. And each time he avoids a positive event—an invitation to dinner, a chance to show his pottery—he reinforces the belief that he has lost himself. The old Ravi, the one who laughed and threw pots for hours, seems gone.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a morning last week when he could not bring himself to enter his studio. The clay was waiting, but the thought of facing the wheel, of feeling any pleasure, felt like a betrayal. He sat in the backyard, watching a car drive past, and he wept. His wife found him there, and for the first time in months, he let her hold his hand. He came to the appointment because he is terrified he will never work again, and because he is equally terrified that working might bring the memories roaring back. He wants to know if there is a way to be safe without hiding for the rest of his life.

violation_explanations: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals (e.g., belief that world is dangerous) directly cause the patient to perceive or notice triggers; rather, triggers lead to appraisals.
No paragraph conveys that the trauma memory directly causes the patient to perceive or notice triggers; instead, triggers evoke memory and maladaptive strategies cause increased sensitivity.
